content: The diagnosis and management of childhood tuberculosis (TB) involve collaboration with pediatricians across the country. Based on 2011 data, children accounted for 0% of reported TB cases in this high-income country, meeting the established standard. TB is a relatively rare disease, with case rates typically expressed per 100,000 population per year. It has a highly variable incubation period, ranging from days to decades after infection, and a relatively low virulence, as only a small proportion of infected individuals develop the disease during their lifetime. TB prevention relies on four key strategies: In countries without vital registration (VR) data, benchmarks must be met to assess TB control standards. These benchmarks include internal consistency over the past five years in the following areas: (1) the ratio of pulmonary to extrapulmonary TB cases, (2) the ratio of male to female TB cases, (3) the proportion of childhood TB cases among all TB cases, (4) year-to-year changes in case notification rates for all forms of TB, (5) year-to-year changes in new smear-positive TB case notification rates, and (6) the ratio of presumptive TB cases to total TB notifications. In high-performing surveillance systems, trends in TB case counts are expected to align with trends in TB mortality. For countries lacking VR data, alternative benchmarks based on routinely collected data are used to assess internal consistency. Year-to-year changes in TB notification rates and case counts by type, sex, and age are generally not expected to vary dramatically. For countries with VR data, a five-year trend analysis using linear regression of log-transformed rates is conducted. The slope of the regression line represents the average rate of change per year, and the direction of the slope indicates the trend. If the slopes for case notification rates and TB mortality rates have the same sign, the benchmark is met. For countries without VR data, expert opinion is often required to interpret results and assess whether benchmarks are met. At least two independent assessors, along with input from the National TB Program (NTP), should evaluate the data. If all agree that the evidence convincingly satisfies the benchmarks, the standard is considered met. In Uganda, for example, data trends satisfied benchmarks for the ratio of pulmonary to extrapulmonary TB cases, the ratio of male to female TB cases, and the ratio of presumptive TB cases to total notifications. However, benchmarks for the proportion of childhood TB cases, year-to-year changes in case notification rates, and smear-positive TB notification rates were not satisfied, indicating partial internal consistency. TB underreporting remains a significant challenge, particularly in endemic settings where reporting is not mandatory, and patients seek care from diverse providers. Underreporting obscures the true burden of TB, limits understanding of patients receiving substandard care, and hinders resource allocation. Legal mandates for TB case reporting are essential, but even with such frameworks, some underreporting is inevitable. In summary, while some benchmarks for TB surveillance and reporting are met in certain settings, others require further investigation and improvement. Addressing gaps in data consistency, underreporting, and surveillance system performance is critical for effective TB control and resource allocation.
